facts.claim: Nilüfer Yanya's "Rid of Me" is a cover of PJ Harvey's song. Polly Jean Harvey is the credited songwriter.
The single was released on 21 September 2022 through ATO Records. It runs 3:37.
Jazzi Bobbi is credited as producer of Yanya's version.
Jazzi Bobbi is Yanya's longtime bandmate. One review says Bobbi built a disorienting, apocalyptic soundscape with echoing whispers, frenzied saxophones and heightened distortion.
The release was Yanya's first since her second album PAINLESS (March 2022, ATO Records), which received Pitchfork's Best New Music tag.
Yanya played the song live on tour in support of Painless before the studio version came out.
Yanya said the song haunted her for years, but in a comforting way. She called it defiant, alien and twisted, and also very romantic despite what some of the lyrics get at.

Yanya said a teacher showed her the PJ Harvey title track when she was 13 or 14. She said she didn't fully understand it until about five years before that interview. She then recorded her own version and plays it often live.
Yanya told Apple Music her obsession with the song began in 2022. She said she sometimes feels more comfortable playing it than her own songs.
Critics said her version stays largely faithful to the original. It adds atmospheric synths and holds back the big flare-up until the very end.

Yanya was born in London in 1995 and grew up in Chelsea. Her parents are visual artists: her mother is of Irish and Barbadian heritage and her father is Turkish. She began posting demos to SoundCloud in 2014 and released her debut album Miss Universe in 2019.

research.lineage: A cover of PJ Harvey's 1993 alt-rock song, reworked by a London indie-rock and art-pop songwriter with atmospheric synths and saxophone.

draft:
The scariest line in **Rid of Me** is also the most tender one. "I beg you, my darling," the narrator sings, and a few breaths later she promises, "I'm gonna twist your head off, see." The song doesn't pick between those two people. It's a plea and a threat from the same mouth, and the pull of it comes from how little distance there is between them.

PJ Harvey wrote it, and her 1993 original is one of the defining howls of alt-rock. Nilüfer Yanya's version keeps that bones-out obsession but changes the temperature. A clean electric guitar picks out an arpeggiated figure with a little reverb on it, a second guitar joins, and the tempo sits at a medium, driving pace that keeps pressing forward. Yanya sings clear and slightly breathy, close to the ear, with no harmonies to soften it. The room sounds natural and a bit raw. The menace doesn't come from volume. It comes from how calm everything sounds while the words get stranger. The version stays mostly faithful to Harvey's, adds atmospheric synths, and saves its big flare-up for the very end. Jazzi Bobbi, Yanya's longtime bandmate, produced it, with frenzied saxophone and heavier distortion pushing into the dread.

Underneath the bodily images and the threats sits a plain confession: "I've been lonely above everything." That line explains the rest. This is someone so afraid of being left that love turns into holding a person in place. The refrain, repeated until it feels like a loop the narrator can't escape, asks whether the lover wishes he'd never met her. It's cruel and wounded at once. She's taunting him, and she's also saying out loud what she fears he already thinks.

Yanya has called the song defiant, alien and twisted, and also very romantic, despite what some of the lyrics get at. That's the right way to hear it. A teacher showed her Harvey's track when she was 13 or 14, and she said it took her years to really understand it. She played it on tour behind *Painless* before this recording came out, and she has said she sometimes feels more at home playing it than her own songs. You can hear that comfort in her steady delivery. She isn't acting out the obsession. She's describing it from the inside, like someone who knows the feeling and isn't ashamed of it.

The song makes you feel how close desperate love sits to danger, and it makes you a little sorry for the person holding on too tight.
